abstract:
Researchers create a multiomic map of human coronary artery disease that links disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

The post Coronary Artery Disease Genetics Map Links Risk Variants to Genes and Cell Types appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Sophia Ktori

content.value:
Researchers headed by a team at Washington University School of Medicine have applied multiomics to create a map that connects genetic variants long associated with coronary artery disease to the genes they impact. The detailed catalog identifies how specific genetic changes play causal roles in coronary artery disease. They say the study is the first to connect inherited genetic variants to their effects in the coronary arteries, and suggest the findings could guide development of new therapies for heart disease.

While the reported study is focused on cardiovascular disease it describes a new approach for understanding, at the molecular level, any genetically complex condition, such as kidney disease, obesity, diabetes or asthma, the investigators suggested. Such molecular understanding could inform on potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

“We now have a map that connects noncoding genetic variants associated with coronary artery disease to the protein-coding genes and cell types they impact, paving the way for possible new therapeutics,” said WashU Medicine cardiologist Nathan O. Stitziel, MD, PhD, a professor of medicine and of genetics. “And because the gene mapping approach we employed could be applied to any complex disease, we think this study could be highly impactful for the field of human genetics broadly.”

Stitziel is senior author of the team’s published paper in Nature, titled “Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease,” in which they wrote, “Collectively, we provide a multiomic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic, and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.”

Common chronic diseases such as coronary artery disease develop via the complex interplay of genetics and environment. Large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified more than 350 inherited genetic changes associated with higher risk of coronary artery disease. Some of these genetic changes are in regions of the genome that carry instructions for making proteins and therefore affect the construction and function of the relevant protein. But for coronary artery disease and other common chronic diseases, nearly all of the associated genetic variants are located in noncoding regions of the genome, making it difficult to determine exactly what they do. “Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways,” the authors wrote.

Many noncoding regions play key roles in directing which proteins are produced and when. Genetic changes to these regions may result in cellular dysregulation, but to date there has been no comprehensive directory that ties variants in noncoding regions to the downstream effects in different cell types that ultimately lead to heart disease. The emergence of multiomic single-cell technologies has created what the team suggests is “a unique opportunity to profile human tissue at unprecedented resolution.”

For their reported study the team harnessed advanced tools to connect the dots between noncoding variants long associated with coronary artery disease and the practical impact these variants have on protein machinery in the coronary arteries. The investigators analyzed 44 coronary artery samples from patients undergoing heart transplantation for heart failure.

Researchers at WashU Medicine have created a detailed map connecting inherited genetic variants to their practical effects in the coronary arteries. Shown is a cross section of a mouse artery with atherosclerotic plaque, similar to what develops in patients with coronary artery disease. Red indicates vascular smooth muscle cells, and green indicates foam cells, which develop from vascular smooth muscle cells and other cell types that have accumulated excess fat and cholesterol. Cell nuclei are in blue. [In-Hyuk Jung]

About half of the patients had heart failure due to blocked coronary arteries and half had heart failure due to other causes. “… we performed single-nucleus multiomic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map,” they explained.

The researchers studied four major cell types present in the coronary arteries: smooth muscle cells, which help the vessels contract; endothelial cells, which line the inside of vessels; fibroblasts, which help provide structure to the vessel; and immune cells, which respond to infections and inflammatory injury.

The researchers found that much of the heritable portion of coronary artery disease risk is in noncoding variants that act on genes in cells of the artery wall, particularly smooth muscle cells. For example, one genetic variant from a noncoding region triggered protein production that caused smooth muscle cells to lose some of their contractile quality, making them stiffer and more inflammatory. Targeting such proteins could lead to new ways to help smooth muscle cells maintain their ability to contract, perhaps keeping the coronary arteries healthier longer.

Stitziel and colleagues are studying several genes identified in this study in efforts to pursue new therapeutics for coronary artery disease. They’re also analyzing more samples of diseased arteries to expand their current genomic map into a larger and more detailed resource for researchers seeking better treatments for coronary artery disease.

“Collectively, we provide a disease agnostic framework to apply human genetic findings to nominate pathologic cell states and genes driving disease, constructing a comprehensive GWAS variant-to-gene map with genetic- and tissue-level convergence for future mechanistic and therapeutic studies,” the authors wrote in summary.
